surface_forms: celle qui m'avait tant charmé et qui n'était plus

appraisal_events.evidence: par un troisième mariage, était princesse de Guermantes et avait dans le faubourg Saint-Germain une grande situation qui eût fort étonné à Combray
appraisal_events.explanation: Through a succession of three marriages Mme Verdurin has attained the title and social position of princesse de Guermantes, a rise the narrator states plainly as a real, striking elevation.

appraisal_events.evidence: Quand elle eut épousé le prince de Guermantes, on dut se dire que c'était un faux Guermantes, un escroc; earlier called out mockingly as 'la duchesse de Duras' as if playing a stage role.
appraisal_events.explanation: Society greets Mme Verdurin's new titles with suspicion and mockery, treating her ascension as illegitimate imposture rather than genuine standing.

status_effects.explanation: She now holds a princely title and a great position in the Faubourg Saint-Germain that would have astonished her Combray-era acquaintances.
Despite the formal elevation, she is mocked and regarded as a fraudulent climber ('faux Guermantes, escroc') by the old social world.
The narrator frames the succession to her name and title as a sorrowful usurpation, likening the dead princess to a defenseless woman being robbed of what was hers.

ambiguities: Per the reference sheet's own note, the bare surface form 'princesse de Guermantes' is genuinely ambiguous across the corpus between the deceased Marie-Gilbert and the current title-holder (Mme Verdurin); within this specific passage the text explicitly disambiguates the two, but the underlying naming collision is itself part of what the passage thematizes.
